newsitem.title: USA: White House details visits by big Clinton fund raiser.
newsitem.headline: White House details visits by big Clinton fund raiser.

text.p: The White House said on Thursday Pauline Kanchanalak, a heavy Clinton campaign contributor with close ties to businesses in Thailand, made at least 26 visits to the White House over the past four years.

The visits by Kanchanalak, who is active in Democratic Party circles, were disclosed in documents sent to Representative Benjamin Gilman, the New York Republican who is chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on International Relations that is looking at Asian contributions to Clinton's campaign.

The Democratic National Committee returned $253,000 of Kanchanalak's contributions after she told the Los Angeles Times last month that the money came from her mother-in-law, Praitun Kanchanalak. It said the contributions were legal.

The documents, which summarize Secret Service records of people cleared to enter the White House, included a cover letter from White House counsel Jack Quinn and were made available to the media by administration officials.

The disclosure was the second time in eight days that the White House has offered details of visits to the White House by people connected with Asian American fundraising for the Clintons and the Democratic Party.

Last Wednesday, the White House said Charles Yan Lin Trie, a Little Rock, Arkansas, restaurateur who raised $640,000 for a legal defence fund for Clinton and his wife Hillary, had visited the White House at least 23 times since January 1993.
The legal defence fund returned the funds, characterising it as "questionable" contributions.

The White House has been under pressure to disclose such visits both by the media and congressional committees because of growing interest in the record fundraising that took place before the Nov. 5 election and in whether any undue influence was exerted by contributors.

Of Kanchanalak's visits -- which took place between Jan. 20, 1993, when Clinton took office, and Nov. 30, 1996 -- 10 were for events Clinton was scheduled to attend and two that Vice President Al Gore was to attend.

Kanchanalak was invited to dinner and coffee twice each and to lunch once, according to the White House documents. Her other visits included a U.S.-Thai Business Council meeting at which Clinton and Thai prime minister were to drop by and two "Democratic National Committee Trustee" receptions.
White House officials said that the records showed that Kanchanalak often brought along others on her visits, including prominent Thai businessmen.

White House special counsel Lannie Davis told reporters that Clinton attended some of these events including the DNC coffees "to express his views on the issues and his vision for the country, to greet his friends, supporters and their guests and sometimes to respond to questions."
But he said that the meetings led to no changes in government policy and that "to the best of our knowledge no funds were solicited by anyone at the White House at White House events."

Quinn, in his cover letter, warned Gilman that the Secret Service records are kept for security purposes, rather than for record-keeping, and therefore may not exactly reflect the visits to the White House.

The DNC told the Federal Election Commission, which oversees campaign fundraising, that it was returning the money despite the fact that the contribution was legal because Praitun Kanchanalak was a legal resident of the United States.
Under U.S. law, foreigners who are legal residents in the United States are permitted to make campaign contributions even though they are not allowed to vote.
